title: Child Development
description: Domains of development, milestones, and the major learning theories (Praxis PLT: Students as Learners).
objectives: Identify the domains of child development and describe typical milestones.
Explain how developmental stages influence student learning and behavior.
Differentiate between typical developmental variation and potential concerns.
Discuss the key concepts of major learning and development theories.
Apply an understanding of child development to plan developmentally appropriate strategies.

blocks.text: How old would you be if you didn't know how old you were?

items: **Physical:** body, brain, gross and fine motor skills.
**Typical, not universal:** milestones describe what most children do around an age, not what every child must do.
**Development is asynchronous:** a student can be advanced cognitively yet socially immature.
**Growth is dynamic:** expect bursts and plateaus.

blocks.title: Match each behavior to its developmental domain

cards.text: A kindergartner learns to cut along a line with scissors.
A second grader sorts shapes by number of sides.
A preschooler starts using full sentences to ask for help.
A fourth grader takes a deep breath and waits their turn instead of shouting out.
A seventh grader argues a rule is unfair because it doesn't apply to everyone equally.
A middle schooler plans the steps of a science project and checks their own work.

blocks.title: Match each milestone to its grade band

cards.text: Begins to hold a pencil with a tripod grasp.
Engages in pretend play with simple roles.
Understands conservation of number and volume.
Peer acceptance becomes highly important; heightened self-consciousness.
Reasons about abstract and hypothetical ideas.
Explores identity and future goals more independently.

blocks.title: PLT tip
blocks.text: "Positive" and "negative" mean adding vs. removing, not good vs. bad.

items: Information moves from the **sensory register** to **working memory** to **long-term memory**.
**Piaget:** children build understanding through four stages, using **assimilation** (fitting new information into existing schema) and **accommodation** (changing schema to fit new information).

**Vygotsky:** the **Zone of Proximal Development** is the gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with help. **Scaffolding** and a **More Knowledgeable Other** help learners cross it.

rows: Learns through senses and movement; develops object permanence.
Uses symbols and language; thinking is egocentric; not yet logical about conservation.
Reasons logically about concrete objects; understands conservation.
Reasons about abstract and hypothetical ideas.

items: **Bruner:** discovery learning; spiral curriculum; enactive, iconic, and symbolic representation.
**Erikson:** initiative vs. guilt (3–5), industry vs. inferiority (6–11), identity vs. role confusion (12–18).
**Kohlberg:** pre-conventional, conventional, and post-conventional moral reasoning.
**Maslow:** hierarchy of needs; why basic needs come before learning.

blocks.title: Key Idea
blocks.text: When we recognize where students are developmentally, we can better support their growth without rushing to judgment or setting inappropriate expectations.

blocks.scenario: Jordan is a first grader. During independent reading, Jordan often gets up, wanders to the window, and taps on other students' desks. When the teacher asks Jordan to sit down, Jordan says, "I'm bored!" and puts their head on the desk. Jordan reads above grade level.

questions.prompt: In the PLT tip on reinforcement, what do "positive" and "negative" refer to?

options.text: Whether the behavior is good or bad
Whether something is added or removed
Whether the student likes the consequence
Whether the consequence is immediate or delayed

questions.explanation: Positive means something is added; negative means something is removed.

questions.prompt: A third grader reads two grade levels above, but struggles to share and take turns. What does this best illustrate?

options.text: The student has a developmental delay across all domains
Development is asynchronous, so a student can be advanced in one domain and still growing in another
Milestones are strict deadlines
The student should skip a grade

questions.explanation: Development is uneven across domains; that is typical, not a red flag.

questions.prompt: A 9-year-old can reason logically about concrete objects and understands conservation. Which Piaget stage is this?

options.text: Sensorimotor
Preoperational
Concrete operational
Formal operational

questions.explanation: Logical reasoning about concrete objects and conservation mark the concrete operational stage (7–11).

questions.prompt: What is the Zone of Proximal Development (Vygotsky)?

options.text: The gap between a student's grade level and their reading level
The gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with help
The physical area of the classroom where students work with a teacher
The stage at which students can think abstractly

questions.explanation: The ZPD is the space between independent and supported performance, where scaffolding helps most.

questions.prompt: According to Erikson, which crisis best matches students ages 6 to 11?

options.text: Initiative vs. guilt
Industry vs. inferiority
Identity vs. role confusion
Trust vs. mistrust

questions.explanation: Ages 6–11 is industry vs. inferiority: building competence and a sense of accomplishment.

questions.prompt: A student who is hungry, feels unsafe, or feels excluded is struggling to focus on learning. Which idea explains this best?

options.text: Maslow's hierarchy: lower needs must be reasonably met before higher ones drive behavior
Bruner's spiral curriculum
Kohlberg's conventional stage
Skinner's shaping

questions.explanation: Maslow: physiological, safety, and belonging needs come before learning.
